column2: What does a table-valued function return?
column3:
A table of rows and columns.
A TVF supplies rows and named columns that a query can filter or join. A scalar function supplies one value instead.
Review source

column2: What input capability distinguishes a table-valued function from a view?
column3:
A table-valued function can accept parameters.
Pass a customer ID directly to a TVF to select that customer's orders. A view has a fixed definition and takes no call arguments.
Review source

column2: Where do you put a TVF call to use its result as input to another SELECT?
column3:
In the FROM clause.
For example, FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001) makes the result available to the rest of the query. A procedure's result set is not directly usable there.
SELECT OrderID
FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001)
WHERE Status = 'Completed';
Review source

column2: How is an inline table-valued function's result defined?
column3:
By one SELECT query following RETURN.
The SELECT after RETURN specifies every row and column of the result. There is no separate return table to fill.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCustomerOrders (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT OrderID, Status, TotalAmount
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
);
Review source

column2: How does SQL Server determine the result columns of an inline TVF without a separate table declaration?
column3:
From the SELECT list's expressions and aliases.
If the SELECT uses Quantity * Price AS LineTotal, the alias names the output column and the expression determines its type.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCustomerOrders (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT OrderID, Status, TotalAmount
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
);
Review source

column2: Which RETURNS clause identifies an inline table-valued function?
column3:
RETURNS TABLE.
RETURNS TABLE declares a table without listing its columns. SQL Server derives them from the SELECT that follows AS RETURN.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCustomerOrders (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT OrderID, Status, TotalAmount
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
);
Review source

column2: How does a multi-statement table-valued function declare its result structure?
column3:
With a named table variable and explicit column definitions in RETURNS.
Declare the return table's name and columns in the header. The function can then insert into that variable before returning it.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source

column2: What table does INSERT INTO @SalesSummary change when @SalesSummary is the TVF's declared return variable?
column3:
The local table variable that becomes the returned table.
The insert fills a table variable local to the function. Rows added to it form the result rather than modifying application data.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source

column2: What result does bare RETURN send back after a multi-statement TVF fills its return table?
column3:
It ends the function and returns the declared result table.
A bare RETURN sends back the table named in the function header. Unlike a scalar UDF, it does not take a value expression.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source

column2: Which table-valued function type supports several procedural statements to build a result table?
column3:
A multi-statement table-valued function.
This form lets you build the returned table in stages. Fabric SQL database supports it, but Fabric Warehouse supports inline TVFs instead.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column2: Why can an inline TVF calculate both COUNT and SUM without a multi-statement body?
column3:
One SELECT query can contain several aggregate expressions.
A single grouped SELECT can calculate COUNT and SUM together. Use an inline function when that one query defines the whole result.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCustomerSummary (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS OrderCount, SUM(TotalAmount) AS Total
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
);
Review source

column2: Why can an inline table-valued function produce better execution plans than a multi-statement function?
column3:
The optimizer can integrate its SELECT query with the calling query.
SQL Server can optimize the inline SELECT together with the caller's joins and filters. That gives it more information but does not guarantee a faster plan.
Review source

column2: What estimate can lead the optimizer to choose a poor join for a multi-statement TVF?
column3:
Its result row count can be estimated poorly.
If the optimizer expects a small result but receives thousands of rows, its chosen join or memory allocation can be a poor fit.
Review source

column2: How can a calling query further filter a table-valued function's returned rows?
column3:
Apply an outer WHERE clause.
Add WHERE Status = 'Completed' to the outer query. It narrows the rows that the customer function returns without changing its definition.
SELECT OrderID
FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001)
WHERE Status = 'Completed';
Review source

column2: Which operator lets a TVF on the right accept a column from each left-side row?
column3:
APPLY.
APPLY lets the right side refer to a column such as c.CustomerID from the left. Choose the APPLY form based on whether to keep unmatched left rows.
SELECT c.CustomerID, o.OrderID
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
CROSS APPLY dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o;
Review source

column2: What happens to a customer row when CROSS APPLY's function returns no orders for it?
column3:
The customer contributes no rows to the result.
For a customer with no returned orders, CROSS APPLY has nothing to pair with that customer. Use OUTER APPLY when the customer must still appear.
SELECT c.CustomerID, o.OrderID
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
CROSS APPLY dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o;
Review source

column2: How does OUTER APPLY handle a customer whose function result is empty?
column3:
It retains the customer with NULLs in the function's output columns.
OUTER APPLY supplies a NULL-extended row when the function returns nothing. A later filter on an order column can still exclude that customer.
SELECT c.CustomerID, o.OrderID
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
OUTER APPLY dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o;
Review source

column2: Each customer row passes the same dates to a product-summary TVF. Why are the totals not customer-specific?
column3:
The call supplies no customer-specific argument.
Every customer supplies the same dates, so the function result has no link to that customer's key. Pass a customer argument or add an appropriate matching condition.
Review source

column2: In SQL Server, what chooses the physical plan for a query written with APPLY?
column3:
The SQL Server query optimizer.
APPLY describes how the two inputs relate. The optimizer chooses the physical plan, so its written form does not force literal per-row execution.
Review source

column2: When can you join a TVF with ordinary JOIN rather than using APPLY for its arguments?
column3:
When its arguments do not depend on the other join input.
A call with a constant can be joined using an ON condition. If the function must receive a column from the left row, use APPLY instead.
SELECT d.OrderID
FROM dbo.OrderDetails AS d
INNER JOIN dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001) AS o
    ON o.OrderID = d.OrderID;
Review source

column2: Where do you put TRY...CATCH to handle an error raised during a TVF call?
column3:
In the calling batch or procedure, not inside the function.
Put the call inside TRY in the caller and handle catchable errors there. A T-SQL function cannot define its own TRY...CATCH block.
Review source

column2: Which SQL Server 2017-and-later feature improves row-count estimates for eligible multi-statement table-valued function queries?
column3:
Interleaved execution.
During eligible optimization, SQL Server executes the function to learn how many rows it returned. Compatibility level 140 or higher makes this available when the feature is enabled.
Review source
